ClinicalDocument.title: SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD — Gynecologic Oncology Referral — Gilda Radner — True-date frame: synthetic events are moved into the patient's historical lifetime. Codes, instruments, and treatments remain modern and are anachronistic.

code.originalText: Four weeks of bloating, early fullness and pelvic pain in a woman of 39: symptom index, pelvic examination, CA-125, and same-week imaging

text.paragraph: Suspected ovarian cancer in a 39-year-old comedian and actor with four weeks of bloating, early fullness, pelvic pain and urinary frequency on most days (ovarian cancer symptom index positive), a firm, fixed right adnexal mass and ascites on examination, a CA-125 of 1240 U/mL, and ovarian cancer in three relatives. Please see her within the week, confirm the diagnosis, and plan her primary treatment. [S]

list.item: Does she have ovarian cancer, and what is its stage?
Is she a candidate for primary cytoreductive surgery, or would chemotherapy before surgery be better?
Which genetic tests should be done, on her blood and on the tumor, and what do the results mean for her and her family?
What chemotherapy and maintenance treatment do you recommend after surgery, and what monitoring should primary care share?
What should be done to prevent blood clots and to support her through treatment?

text.paragraph: Four weeks of bloating that makes her clothes tight, feeling full after a few bites, a dull lower abdominal and pelvic ache, and passing urine more often, on most days; tired for longer than that. Never carried a pregnancy to term: two early losses and one unsuccessful IVF cycle. Ashkenazi Jewish ancestry; ovarian cancer in her grandmother, an aunt and a cousin, and her father died of a brain tumor; no genetic testing in the family is known. Examination today: distended abdomen with shifting dullness and a firm, fixed, irregular right adnexal mass. Results today: CA-125 1240 U/mL, CEA 1.6 ng/mL, hemoglobin 12.4 g/dL, platelets 412, creatinine 0.72 mg/dL, albumin 3.6 g/dL. Transvaginal ultrasound and CT of the chest, abdomen and pelvis booked this week, with image-guided biopsy if the scan shows disease outside the pelvis. PHQ-2 negative. No medicines; no known allergies. She is frightened that this is cancer and wants to be told plainly [S]

list.item: Four weeks of bloating that makes her clothes tight, feeling full after a few bites, a dull ache low in the abdomen and pelvis, and passing urine more often, on most days; she has been more tired than usual for longer than that. [S]
Afraid this is cancer: her father died of a brain tumor and ovarian cancer runs in her family; she wants to be taken seriously and told plainly. [S]

text.paragraph: Historical basis. These claims are historical evidence, not findings from a modern examination.

list.item: Gilda Radner was born on June 28, 1946, into a prosperous Detroit Jewish family; her paternal grandfather had emigrated from Lithuania. [D]

She was the first person cast in Saturday Night Live, performed with its original troupe from 1975 to 1980, won an Emmy Award in 1978, and made several films, including three with Gene Wilder, whom she married in 1984. [D]
Her father died of brain cancer when she was fourteen. Her grandmother, a cousin, and an aunt had all had ovarian cancer. [D]

Her illness began with severe fatigue, which sources date to the filming of Haunted Honeymoon in England in 1985 or to early 1986; her internist attributed it to Epstein-Barr virus and told her not to worry. [D]

Before her illness she and her husband tried to have a child; she had two miscarriages, one during the filming of Haunted Honeymoon in London, and an unsuccessful round of in vitro fertilization, after which doctors told her she was infertile. [D]
During her Saturday Night Live years her lifelong insecurity about her appearance resurfaced in bouts of bulimia, which she later wrote about. [D]

text.paragraph: 6 later historical claims are omitted because they describe events after the index age. See the teaching note.
No medications started by this date.

At the first visit: the ovarian cancer symptom index, an abdominal and pelvic examination, CA-125 with CEA, blood count and chemistry, and a urine pregnancy test; transvaginal ultrasound and CT of the chest, abdomen and pelvis within the week, and image-guided biopsy if the scan shows disease outside the pelvis. Guideline: NCCN Clinical Practice Guidelines in Oncology: Ovarian Cancer/Fallopian Tube Cancer/Primary Peritoneal Cancer, Version 4.2026 (2026); Goff BA, et al. Development of an ovarian cancer symptom index: possibilities for earlier detection. Cancer 2007;109(2):221-227 (2007); Committee Opinion No. 716: The Role of the Obstetrician-Gynecologist in the Early Detection of Epithelial Ovarian Cancer in Women at Average Risk (2017) [S]
